model-knowledge.note: Seed pending harvest; Wikipedia and vendor spec sources egress-blocked in this environment.

records.name: Counter-Strike 2
records.notes: Valve publishes a thread floor (4 hardware threads) rather than a core floor, so minCores is null. No official deterministic benchmark ships with the game; reviewers use community workshop maps or demo playback. FSR 1.0 is exposed in the video options.

records.name: Valorant
records.notes: Deliberately low-spec target (min GPU is Intel HD 4000). No vendor upscaler; render-scale only.

records.name: Dota 2
records.notes: Reviewers benchmark via replay playback rather than a shipped benchmark mode, so builtInBenchmark is false.

records.name: League of Legends
records.notes: DX11 renderer added 2020; DX9 path retained. Lowest GPU load in the catalogue.

records.name: Rainbow Six Siege
records.notes: Deterministic built-in benchmark, one of the most reliable in the suite. Requirements are the original 2015 published minimums; the 2025 Siege X revision may have raised them.

records.name: Overwatch 2
records.notes: Engine frame limiter tops out at 600 fps. FSR 1.0 in graphics options.

records.name: Apex Legends
records.notes: fps_max is clamped at 300 by the engine even when set to unlimited. DX12 renderer added 2023.

records.name: Fortnite
records.notes: Migrated to UE5 with Nanite/Lumen in the DX12 path, but the DX11 Performance mode keeps the hard floor low, so no mesh-shader gate. minVramGB null because the published minimum GPU is an iGPU with shared memory. vramDemandGB is for the Epic/Lumen DX12 preset.

records.name: PUBG Battlegrounds
records.notes: FSR 1.0 support added post-launch; medium confidence.

records.name: Rocket League
records.notes: UE3-era renderer; trivially GPU-light, effectively always CPU/draw-call bound.

records.name: Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024
records.notes: Streaming-first architecture; a large share of frame time is network/asset streaming, so on-GPU demand varies with scenery density. CPU and VRAM floors nulled: I could not confirm the published 2024 minimums (the 2020 table is different and would be wrong here).

records.name: Cities Skylines II
records.notes: Unusually GPU-heavy for a city builder because of HDRP and unculled LODs at launch; late-game is simulation/CPU bound. VRAM figures are among my least certain.

records.name: Factorio
records.notes: Command-line --benchmark runs a save deterministically for N ticks; the cleanest reproducible fixture in the catalogue, but it measures UPS not FPS. Render rate is bounded by the fixed 60 UPS update rate. VRAM is sprite-atlas dominated so it barely scales with resolution; published min GPU VRAM is 512MB, rounded to 1.

records.name: Stellaris
records.notes: Late-game performance is single-thread and memory-latency bound; frame rate is a poor proxy for the thing users actually feel (daily tick rate).

records.name: Total War Warhammer III
records.notes: Ships both a battle and a campaign benchmark; the battle benchmark is GPU-weighted and the campaign one CPU-weighted, so fixtures must record which was used. Published minimum GPU is given as a family (GTX 900 / RX 400) with no VRAM figure, hence null.

records.name: Anno 1800
records.notes: Built-in benchmark exists but is far lighter than a real late-game save, which is heavily CPU bound. Treat benchmark numbers as an optimistic bound.

records.name: Civilization VII
records.notes: builtInBenchmark set false conservatively: Civ V and VI both shipped graphics and AI benchmarks and VII plausibly does too, but I could not confirm it, and a false negative only excludes it from the harness suite whereas a false positive corrupts the fixture set. Requirements largely nulled.

records.name: Escape from Tarkov
records.notes: Year is the closed-beta release. Streets of Tarkov is the worst case by a wide margin and is what the VRAM figures target; other maps are 1.5-2GB lighter. System RAM, not VRAM, is the usual limiter (16GB+ in practice).

records.name: Star Citizen
records.notes: Perpetual alpha with no 1.0; year is the persistent-universe alpha. Performance is dominated by server tick and streaming, so any fitted client-side model has large residuals. VRAM figures are the least reliable in the catalogue.

records.name: ARMA Reforger
records.notes: CPU floors nulled: the published minimum names a 6-core part but I am not confident enough to risk a false CORE_FLOOR gate. upscalingSupport is one of my least certain fields here.

records.name: Red Dead Redemption 2
records.notes: Built-in benchmark is multi-scene and deterministic. Vulkan is generally the faster path and fixtures must record which API was used.

records.name: Horizon Forbidden West
records.notes: Year is the PC release. Sits close to the 8GB cliff at 1440p Very High, so its VRAM numbers matter more than most aaa-raster entries.

records.name: God of War Ragnarok
records.notes: Year is the PC release. Well-optimised corridor-ish rendering; low VRAM pressure for a 2024 port.

records.name: Baldur's Gate 3
records.notes: Act 3 (Lower City) is heavily CPU bound and is not represented by any early-game fixture; archetype aaa-raster understates its CPU weight there.

records.name: Elden Ring
records.notes: Hard 60fps engine cap: every build above the 60fps threshold is engine-cap limited, which the limiter field must report rather than claiming GPU headroom. No vendor upscaler even after the RT patch. Published min RAM of 12GB is unusual and is correct.

records.name: The Witcher 3 Next-Gen
records.notes: Requirements are the next-gen (v4.x) published minimums and are conservative: the retained DX11 path runs far below them, so these floors will over-gate old builds that in practice play the game fine. vramDemandGB is the raster ultra path; the DX12 RT modes are materially higher.

records.name: Forza Horizon 5
records.notes: Excellent deterministic built-in benchmark and very consistent frame pacing; one of the best-behaved fixtures in the core loop. Extreme preset at 4K pushes well past these figures.

records.name: Shadow of the Tomb Raider
records.notes: Long-standing review-suite standard: the built-in benchmark reports CPU and GPU bound frame rates separately, which makes it unusually valuable for fitting the CPU/GPU split. Optional RT shadows are off in the raster reference preset.

records.name: Hitman World of Assassination
records.notes: Year is the WoA rebrand; the engine build lineage is Hitman 3 (2021). Ships two benchmark scenes (Dubai, Dartmoor) with very different CPU weighting, so fixtures must record which.

records.name: Ghost of Tsushima
records.notes: Year is the PC Director's Cut. Nixxes port with a built-in benchmark; unusually efficient VRAM behaviour for a 2024 open world.

records.name: Starfield
records.notes: minShaderModel deliberately null: the game's real requirement is Shader Model 6.6, which cannot be expressed in this catalogue's shader-model vocabulary without falsely gating Pascal, and Pascal (GTX 1070 Ti) is the published minimum GPU. Cities are CPU bound well below the archetype's raster assumption.

records.name: Assassin's Creed Shadows
records.notes: Has a hardware-RT global illumination path with a raster fallback, so it is classified aaa-raster at the reference preset; with RTGI forced on it behaves like an aaa-rt title. Recent title, so both requirements and VRAM figures carry above-average uncertainty.

records.name: Cyberpunk 2077
records.notes: RT is optional, so rayTracingRequired is false; the reference preset for this archetype assumes RT on but not path tracing, which is a much larger load again. Requirements are the post-2.0 published minimums.

records.name: F1 24
records.notes: Built-in benchmark with fixed weather and grid, so it is very repeatable. RT reflections/shadows are optional and lighter than most aaa-rt entries, which makes this the low anchor of the archetype.

records.name: Metro Exodus Enhanced Edition
records.notes: Hard ray-tracing gate: the Enhanced Edition removed the raster lighting path entirely and will not launch without a hardware-RT GPU. This is the canonical RAY_TRACING_REQUIRED case, the counterpart to Alan Wake 2's mesh-shader gate. Ships a standalone benchmark executable.

records.name: Far Cry 6
records.notes: Figures exclude the optional HD texture pack, which Ubisoft itself gates behind 11GB+ VRAM and which would roughly double 4K demand. Any fixture must record whether the HD pack was installed.

records.name: Watch Dogs Legion
records.notes: Ultra textures are the VRAM driver here, not RT; the ultra texture setting alone is what pushes 8GB cards into stutter at 1440p.

records.name: Spider-Man 2
records.notes: Year is the PC port. Traversal streaming makes 1% lows far more informative than averages, and RT reflections are the dominant GPU cost. CPU floors nulled - I could not confirm the published minimum CPUs.

records.name: Black Myth Wukong
records.notes: A standalone benchmark tool was released separately from the game, which makes this an unusually clean fixture. Classified aaa-rt rather than ue5 because full RT is the headline load, but it is a UE5 title and TSR is available.

records.name: Alan Wake 2
records.notes: THE canonical mesh-shader gate: the renderer requires mesh shader support, so Pascal, Maxwell, GCN and RDNA 1 cards produce MESH_SHADER_REQUIRED and no FPS estimate at all. minDxFeatureLevel 12_2 is set to match (Turing+/RDNA2+/Arc) and is consistent with the mesh-shader flag rather than an independent gate. minShaderModel left null so the mesh-shader capability is the single authority. RT is optional (path tracing is a separate tier), so rayTracingRequired is false. No built-in benchmark.

records.name: Remnant II
records.notes: Designed around upscaling: the published targets assume an upscaler is on, so native-resolution estimates will look worse than the developer's own framing. Nanite-heavy, Lumen software GI by default.

records.name: Stalker 2
records.notes: Open-world A-Life simulation gives it a heavier CPU component than the ue5 archetype assumes; expect systematic residuals on weak CPUs.

records.name: Silent Hill 2 (2024)
records.notes: Bloober remake, not the 2001 original. Heavy Lumen use in fog; traversal stutter is a shader-compilation artefact that a mean-FPS model cannot represent.

records.name: Hellblade II
records.notes: Renders at a fixed cinematic aspect with letterboxing, so effective pixel count is below the nominal resolution and the resolution-scaling term will overstate GPU load unless corrected. Very narrow, linear scenes mean an unusually light CPU load.

records.name: The Finals
records.notes: Server-authoritative destruction physics makes it far more CPU sensitive than the ue5 archetype implies, and late-round destruction is not represented by any early-round fixture. minSystemRamGB nulled - I could not confirm the published figure.

records.name: The Last of Us Part I
records.notes: The archetype's reference case: 1440p Ultra genuinely exceeds 8GB, so 8GB cards fall off a cliff rather than degrading smoothly. Post-launch patches reduced demand somewhat from the release-day figures; these are the patched-state estimates and still carry the widest error bars in the catalogue. Has a built-in benchmark.

records.name: Hogwarts Legacy
records.notes: 1440p Ultra exceeds 8GB; Hogsmeade is both the VRAM and the CPU worst case and is the only location worth using as a fixture. Enabling RT raises demand by roughly another 1.5-2GB. No built-in benchmark despite being in the core loop.

records.name: Ratchet and Clank Rift Apart
records.notes: Year is the PC port. Lower demand than the other vram-heavy entries because the streaming system is genuinely good, but it is DirectStorage-dependent and degrades badly on HDD, which is a storage effect the model does not represent.

records.name: Call of Duty Black Ops 6
records.notes: Texture streaming is adaptive and will consume most of whatever VRAM is available, so a measured allocation figure overstates true demand; these numbers are intended as the working-set requirement, not the allocation. That makes them hard to validate against review data.

records.name: Diablo IV
records.notes: Published minimum spec is very low, but the Ultra texture quality preset was notorious at launch for exceeding 8GB cards at 4K; the gap between the minimum spec and the reference-preset demand is the largest of any entry here.
